title: both / both of; neither / neither of; either / either of
subtitle: both / neither / either (of)
summary: Use both, neither and either to talk about two things, with or without of, and pair them as both ... and, neither ... nor, either ... or.

lesson.heading: both / neither / either + noun
lesson.text: We use **both / neither / either** for two things. Imagine you are going out to eat and there are two possible restaurants.

examples.text: We can go to **either** restaurant. I don't mind.
examples.note: = one or the other, it doesn't matter which

examples.text: I haven't been to **either** restaurant before.

lesson.heading: both / neither / either without a noun
lesson.text: You can also use these words alone, for example as short answers.

examples.text: 'Which do you prefer, basketball or tennis?' 'It's hard to say. I like **both**.'
'Is your friend British or American?' '**Neither**. She's Australian.'
'Do you want tea or coffee?' '**Either**. I don't mind.'

lesson.heading: both of / neither of / either of + the / these / my ...
lesson.text: Before **the, these, those, my, Tom's** etc. we use **both of / neither of / either of**. We say 'both of the restaurants' (but not 'both of restaurants'). After **both** you can leave out of.

examples.text: **Neither of the** restaurants we went to was expensive.
I haven't been to **either of those** restaurants.
**Both of these** restaurants are good. or **Both these** restaurants are good.

lesson.heading: both of / neither of / either of + us / you / them
lesson.text: Before **us, you, them** you must use **of** - also after both. After **neither of** the verb can be singular or plural.

examples.text: I asked two people how to get to the station, but **neither of them** knew.
Neither of them **is** at home. or Neither of them **are** at home.

lesson.heading: both ... and / neither ... nor / either ... or
rows: Both Chris and Paul were late. / I was both tired and hungry when I arrived home.
Neither Chris nor Paul came to the party. / There was an accident outside our house, but we neither saw nor heard anything.
I'm not sure where Maria's from. She's either Spanish or Italian. / Either you apologise, or I'll never speak to you again.

left.label: Two things: either / neither / both
examples: There are two good hotels here. You could stay at **either of them**.
We tried two hotels. **Neither of them** had a room.

right.label: More than two: any / none / all
examples: There are many good hotels here. You could stay at **any of them**.
We tried a lot of hotels. **None of them** had a room.

lesson.text: both / neither / either = exactly two. For three or more, switch to all / none / any.

exercises.prompt: 'What day is it today - the 18th or the 19th?' '___. It's the 20th.'
exercises.explanation: Not one and not the other of the two: Neither.

exercises.prompt: 'Where did you go on your trip - Korea or Japan?' 'We went to ___. A week in Korea and a week in Japan.'
'Shall we sit in the corner or by the window?' '___. I don't mind.'
exercises.explanation: One or the other, it doesn't matter which: Either.

exercises.prompt: ___ Tom's parents is English. His father is Polish and his mother is Italian.
exercises.explanation: Before Tom's we need of, and the meaning is 'not one and not the other': Neither of Tom's parents.

exercises.prompt: I was invited to two parties last week, but I couldn't go to ___.
exercises.explanation: After a negative verb (couldn't) we use either: not ... either of them = neither of them.

exercises.prompt: Sam and I often play tennis, but we're not very good. ___ can play well.
exercises.explanation: Not one and not the other of two people, with a positive verb: Neither of us.

exercises.prompt: It was a boring movie. It was long too. Make one sentence with both ... and.
exercises.answer: The movie was both boring and long.

exercises.prompt: Joe doesn't have a car. Sam doesn't have one either. Make one sentence with neither ... nor.
exercises.answer: Neither Joe nor Sam has a car.
exercises.explanation: neither ... nor ... joins two negative ideas, and the verb is positive (has).
Both restaurants are good. We do not say the both.

exercises.prompt: Emily has four brothers, but I haven't met ___ of them.
exercises.explanation: Four brothers = more than two, so any (not either).

exercises.prompt: Match each pair of sentences with the single sentence that means the same.

pairs.left: Emily speaks German and she speaks Russian too.
pairs.right: Emily speaks both German and Russian.

pairs.left: Ben doesn't watch TV and he doesn't read newspapers.
pairs.right: Ben neither watches TV nor reads newspapers.

pairs.left: I don't have time to go on holiday. And I don't have the money.
pairs.right: I have neither the time nor the money to go on holiday.

pairs.left: We can leave today or we can leave tomorrow - whichever you prefer.
pairs.right: We can leave either today or tomorrow.

pairs.left: Is that man's name Richard? Or is it Robert? It's one of the two.
pairs.right: That man's name is either Richard or Robert.

exercises.prompt: Is the speaker talking about two things or about more than two?

items.text: You could stay at either of them.
None of them had a room.
Neither of them knew the way.
Have you been to any of these countries?
